terms.grammar: adverb; mostly after a negative, in conditions and in questions
evidence: Ter. Eun. 852: sī aliam admīserō umquam, occīditō
terms.comment: “Never” is numquam, and “not … ever” nec umquam, nēmō umquam. “Ever since” is ex quō or ūsque ab (Traupman 379).

terms.gloss: ever (asking about a time not fixed); at some time
evidence: Plin. Ep. 8.8.1: vīdistīne aliquandō Clitumnum fontem?
terms.comment: Where umquam belongs to denials and doubt, aliquandō belongs to plain statements and open questions (Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: indefinite adverb: sī quandō, if ever
evidence: Mor. 67: sī quandō vacuum casula pluviaeve tenēbant
Catull. 84.1: sī quandō commoda vellet dīcere

phrases.latin: cūrā ut valeās et ita tibi persuādeās, mihi tē cārius nihil esse nec umquam fuisse
phrases.english: look after yourself, and be sure that nothing is or ever was dearer to me than you
have you ever seen the spring of Clitumnus?

phrases.latin: Ūnam hanc noxiam mitte: sī aliam admīserō umquam, occīditō.
phrases.english: Let this one fault go: if I ever do another, kill me.

aliquando.html: A compound of quandō, which de Vaan gives with a long final vowel (p. 507, s.v. quī); Festus records an older form quandōd (Lewis & Short s.v. quando). The Latinitas loci write aliquandō throughout, and the libellī quandō.

sources: Lewis & Short: umquam · Lewis & Short: aliquando · Lewis & Short: quando
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 379. Michiel de Vaan, Etymological Dictionary of Latin and the other Italic Languages (2008), p. 507.

Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-cicero-epistulae, loci-plinius, loci-seneca-epistulae, loci-vergilius, loci-catullus), checked against the editions named there; Terence (Eun. 851–852) checked against the Perseus Latin texts.
